newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Tight EU budgets set off worker discontent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tight EU budgets set off worker discontent.

text.p: Attempts to instill some fiscal discipline into European economies ahead of a single currency have been sending protesters out onto the streets from Athens to the Pas de Calais.
In Greece, farmers have blockaded roads and railways for 12 days in protest against government plans to end tax breaks worth some 130 billion drachmas ($520 million).
Spanish civil servants have called a 24-hour strike for Wednesday in reaction to plans to freeze their 1997 salaries.
A German law to allow companies to cut sick pay entitlements has triggered mass protests, discouraging firms from applying the law.
Last month, half-a-million Italians marched in Rome in opposition to a Euro-tax designed to help Italy qualify for the new European Union currency.

Most spectacularly, French lorry drivers clogged road across their country, causing nightmarish backups even across the English Channel -- all to get an earlier retirement and a ban on Sunday driving.

The protests have little in common individually, but the trigger for many of them can be traced to the feverish attempts by European Union countries to get their economies ready for economic and monetary union (EMU).

To participate in EMU -- or more specifically, the third phase of EMU, the single currency -- requires countries to lower their budget deficits to no more than three percent of gross domestic product.

Countries will be judged on whether they have done this in early 1998, based on their performance in 1997. Hence, budgets being put in place today are tight, hurting or threatening to hurt those reaching for their protest placards.

In Spain, for example, the civil servants are livid with the conservative government for trying to freeze their salaries -- a move Madrid says will save 200 billion pesetas ($1.53 billion) from the deficit.

The Italian march, organised by the main centre-right opposition, was aimed at the government's proposed one-off Euro-tax, a revenue raiser that has also raised a few eyebrows at central banks concerned about the sustainability of post-EMU financial discipline.
In Greece, which has next to no chance of meeting the single currency criteria on time to be among the first to adopt it, the government is struggling to prepare the way for a later entry.

It has announced new taxes and the abolition of tax breaks, but farmers, with a list of economic demands, have paralysed road and rail links, blocking nearly 100 points around Greece and causing chaos for international and domestic transport.
Tensions are also growing in other countries over government plans involving both the single currency and attempts to render labour markets more flexible.
Unions and the government in Portugal are in tight negotiations over a pay increase for 500,000 public sector employees.
In Germany, meanhile, the sick pay cuts are part a package designed to lower productions costs and make German companies more competitive.
